column1: The world's oldest company ran for over 1,400 years
column2: Kongō Gumi, a Japanese temple builder, was founded in 578 AD. It traded independently until 2006, when it was absorbed by a larger construction firm.
column3: Longevity comes from doing one thing well for a very long time.

column1: Coca-Cola was first sold as a medicine
column2: In 1886 pharmacist John Pemberton sold Coca-Cola in Atlanta as a tonic at soda fountains. It became a mass-market drink through marketing, not medicine.
column3: Products often find their real market by accident.

column1: Nokia started as a paper mill
column2: Nokia was founded in Finland in 1865 as a pulp mill. Over the next century it moved into rubber, cables and finally mobile phones.
column3: Companies can reinvent themselves many times.

column1: The first barcode scanned was on chewing gum
column2: On 26 June 1974, a pack of Wrigley's gum was the first product scanned by a UPC barcode at a supermarket in Ohio.
column3: Huge systems often start with a humble test.

column1: Post-it Notes came from a failed glue
column2: A 3M scientist created a weak, reusable adhesive in 1968 that nobody could find a use for. Years later a colleague used it to stop bookmarks falling out of his hymn book.
column3: A failure in one context can be a hit in another.

column1: Supermarkets put milk at the back for a reason
column2: Essentials like milk are often placed at the far end of the store so shoppers pass more products on the way. Each extra aisle is another chance to buy.
column3: Store layouts are designed, not accidental.

column1: The 80/20 rule started with peas
column2: Economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that 20 percent of the pea pods in his garden produced most of the peas. He then found that about 20 percent of people owned 80 percent of land in Italy.
column3: Uneven distributions show up everywhere.

column1: Prices ending in 99 really work
column2: Studies find that prices like £4.99 often sell better than £5.00 because shoppers anchor on the first digit. This is called the left-digit effect.
column3: Small framing changes move big decisions.

column1: Lego nearly went bankrupt in 2003
column2: After expanding into too many products, Lego faced heavy losses. It recovered by refocusing on its core bricks and cutting complexity.
column3: Focus can rescue a company that sprawled.

column1: Amazon started as an online bookshop
column2: When it launched in 1995, Amazon sold only books. Books were easy to ship and had a huge catalogue no physical store could stock.
column3: Start narrow, then expand.

column1: Monopoly was originally a warning about landlords
column2: The game began as The Landlord's Game, patented by Lizzie Magie in 1904 to show how land ownership concentrated wealth. Later versions dropped the message.
column3: Ideas can be repackaged to mean the opposite.

column1: The first credit card was for restaurants
column2: Diners Club launched in 1950 as a card for paying at restaurants in New York. It was a charge card, paid off in full each month.
column3: Big financial products often start in one niche.

column1: Free shipping thresholds raise basket size
column2: Many shoppers add items just to reach a free delivery threshold. Retailers set the line slightly above the typical order.
column3: Thresholds nudge behaviour more than discounts.

column1: The decoy effect sells more large drinks
column2: When a medium option priced close to the large is added, more people choose the large. The middle option exists mainly to make the big one look good value.
column3: Options can be designed to steer a choice.

column1: Netflix once mailed DVDs
column2: Netflix began in 1997 as a DVD-by-post rental service. It started streaming in 2007 and kept mailing discs until 2023.
column3: The winning business model may grow inside the old one.

column1: The stock market's opening bell is a real bell
column2: The New York Stock Exchange rings a bell to open and close trading each weekday. Guests ring it as a publicity event.
column3: Rituals help markets feel orderly.

column1: Compound interest is called the eighth wonder
column2: Money growing at 7 percent a year doubles roughly every 10 years. Starting earlier matters more than starting bigger.
column3: Time is the most powerful input.

column1: Most new restaurants struggle in their first years
column2: Studies of restaurant openings find a large share close within the first few years. Thin margins and high fixed costs leave little room for error.
column3: Passion needs a business model behind it.

column1: Logos rarely use purple
column2: Purple is among the least common main colours in big-brand logos; blue and red dominate. Colour choices signal trust, energy or luxury.
column3: Colour is part of the message.

column1: Shipping containers changed world trade
column2: Standard steel containers, introduced in 1956, cut the cost and time of loading ships dramatically. Global trade grew as a result.
column3: A boring standard can transform an industry.

column1: The paperclip has a surprisingly rich history
column2: The familiar double-loop Gem paperclip appeared in Britain in the 1870s and was never patented in its classic form. Many tried to improve it, but the design endured.
column3: Good enough can be unbeatable.

column1: Bubble wrap was meant to be wallpaper
column2: Inventors in 1957 tried to sell textured plastic as wallpaper. It failed, then found its use protecting fragile goods in shipping.
column3: Keep looking for the job your product does best.

column1: Sunk costs trap good decision-makers
column2: People keep investing in failing projects because of money already spent. The rational choice looks only at future costs and benefits.
column3: Past spending should not decide future spending.

column1: A small loss feels bigger than an equal gain
column2: Research by Kahneman and Tversky found losses weigh roughly twice as heavily as gains of the same size. This is called loss aversion.
column3: Framing a choice as a loss changes behaviour.

column1: Ford's moving assembly line cut build time sharply
column2: In 1913 Ford's moving line cut the time to build a Model T chassis from about 12 hours to around 90 minutes. Prices fell and sales soared.
column3: Process innovation can matter more than product.
